title: Timbuktu's manuscripts
hook: a city of scholars, with the Sankore mosque and its manuscripts kept in family libraries

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mansa Musa's Hajj, a king who gave so much that gold lost its value, and borrowed to get home. Your line was the richest pilgrim.

In English, "from here to Timbuktu" means the end of the earth, a place so far away it might as well be invented. But Timbuktu is real. It sits near the bend of the Niger, at the edge of the desert. In its mud-brick houses, families kept wooden chests and cupboards full of handwritten books, some pages brittle and brown, with notes squeezed into the margins. A traveler known as Leo Africanus passed through and noticed something strange about the market: books were among the most valuable things for sale. Today: Timbuktu's manuscripts.
screen: `THE END OF THE EARTH?` → `A REAL TOWN ON THE NIGER.` → `CHESTS FULL OF HANDWRITTEN BOOKS.`

segments.voice: One surah of the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, is named al-Qalam, the Pen, and it opens with an oath. In Pickthall's translation: "Nun. By the pen and that which they write (therein)." Timbuktu took the pen seriously. Leo Africanus wrote that the town had many judges, teachers and learned men, paid by the king, and that handwritten books brought from North Africa sold there for more than any other merchandise. Scholars gathered at mosques like Sankore, and students sat with teachers one book at a time, often copying the book for themselves as they studied it. What's in the manuscripts? Copies of the Qur'an, yes. But also law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, Sufi poetry, astronomy for setting prayer times, medicine, letters between scholars, records of sales and debts and marriages. A whole town's mind, written down. The chronicler al-Sa'di remembers the scholar Ahmad Baba, who was carried away from Timbuktu into exile after Moroccan forces took the city. Tradition says he mourned the books he lost. Families kept the rest, generation after generation, and tradition says some were hidden in walls or buried in the sand. And in recent years, when armed men held the town, librarians and families carried manuscripts away to safety in trunks. Gold passed through Timbuktu. The pages stayed.
screen: `BY THE PEN AND WHAT THEY WRITE.` · `BOOKS WORTH MORE THAN OTHER GOODS.` · `LAW, STARS, MEDICINE, LETTERS.` · `KEPT, HIDDEN, CARRIED TO SAFETY.` · then, large: `THE CITY OF MANUSCRIPTS.`

segments.voice: Go back over what the chests held: law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, poetry, the stars, medicine, letters, records of debts and marriages, and let one of them catch your interest. Suppose a family in Timbuktu lifted the lid and let you read a single page on it: what would you hope to find out? If you pray, give thanks for the scholars who wrote and the families who kept; if not, simply hold the question.
Timbuktu's manuscripts. The handwritten books of a West African city of scholars, on law, faith, stars and medicine, kept by families and carried to safety. Today's word.
Your line: the city of manuscripts. Kept in chests, in walls, and in trunks, for centuries. That's day nine hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Families and libraries in Timbuktu still keep manuscripts, and scholars and conservators work to preserve, catalog and photograph them so they can be read.
